Idiopathic Disorders of the CNS

Neuro · Week 4
LO 1–5 Chronic communicating hydrocephalus 3 Ws: Wet, Wacky, Wobbly Shunt-responsive

💧 Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus

▶
▶ Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus \ everything you need to know
Video — "Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus \ everything you need to know" (YouTube)
📺 Supplementary resource: Osmosis — Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus
🎯 How boards would word it

A 74-year-old man is brought in by his family for evaluation of a 6-month history of progressively unsteady walking, several recent falls, and new urinary urgency with occasional incontinence. His family also notes he seems more forgetful and apathetic than before. On exam he has a wide-based, shuffling gait with difficulty initiating steps, though strength and sensation are normal. There is no papilledema. Brain MRI shows ventricular enlargement out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

Increased ventricular volume with concomitant specific neurological signs (gait abnormalities, incontinence, dementia) in the setting of normal opening lumbar CSF pressure — a form of chronic communicating hydrocephalus. Synonyms: NPH, occult/adult/idiopathic hydrocephalus, "water-on-the-brain."

  • Not rare — estimated 10–22 per 100,000 overall in the US
  • ~0.2% of the population age 70–79, rising to ~6% of those >80
  • International estimates: ~1 per 25,000, or up to 6% of dementia patients
  • Typically affects individuals ≥50 (classically >60)
  • Slow ventricular enlargement with CSF pressure compensating in the high-normal range
Etiology
  • Idiopathic (iNPH) is the most common form in adults >60
  • Secondary causes — obstruction/fibrosis of subarachnoid villi from CNS inflammatory disease (e.g. meningitis), intraventricular hemorrhage, or subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • Risk factors: stroke, head injury, meningitis, brain tumor, hypertension, diabetes mellitus
Pathophysiology & Pathology

↓CSF absorption → CSF accumulation → ventricular enlargement. ICP stays normal or only mildly elevated because gradual ventricular dilation compensates for the slow CSF accumulation (contrast with an acute process, which would overwhelm this compensation).

  • Elevated venous resistance in stenotic venous sinuses may back up pressure into the cranium; CSF may absorb into periventricular white matter instead of raising ICP significantly
  • Reduced cerebral blood flow under these pressure dynamics → decreased oxygenation may explain clinical symptoms; resulting anoxia may increase neuroinflammation and neuron loss
  • Pathology: enlarged ventricles and sulci, periventricular hyperintensities, wide Sylvian fissure with narrowed high-convexity subarachnoid spaces (disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space — DESH pattern)
Ventricle comparison — normal pressure vs. communicating hydrocephalus vs. obstructive hydrocephalus
2 · Clinical Presentation
Hakim's Triad — "The 3 Ws"

Nota bene: the full triad is a late development and is generally not seen in early stages.

  • Wobbly — slowly progressive gait disorder (90% of patients): unsteadiness, impaired balance, falls; wide-based, reeling gait with hesitancy to lift the feet off the floor ("magnetic gait," gait apraxia)
  • Wacky — impaired mental function (80%): apathy, dullness, inattention, memory loss, short attention span, loss of motivation, spatial disorientation
  • Wet — sphincteric incontinence (45–90%): initially urgency/frequency, progressing to urge incontinence. Mechanism: ventricular dilation distorts corona radiata fibers → loss of inhibition of detrusor activity. Worsens as cognition declines and gait impairment makes reaching the toilet harder

NPH does not cause signs of elevated ICP (no headache, no papilledema) — an important negative finding.

Summary — gradual CSF accumulation causes ventricular enlargement, producing dementia, magnetic gait, and urinary incontinence; a lumbar puncture removing 30–50mL CSF helps confirm the diagnosis
3 · Diagnostic Testing
Diagnostic Approach
  • MRI brain (preferred) or CT head: ventriculomegaly without, or out of proportion to, sulcal enlargement; no evidence of CSF flow obstruction; periventricular white matter changes often seen
  • CSF tap test: lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement, followed by removal of 30–50mL CSF. Opening pressure typically normal or mildly elevated (5–18 mmHg). Gait is assessed before and after — improvement supports the diagnosis and predicts shunt response
  • CSF analysis: to assess for secondary causes (e.g. chronic meningitis)
T1 MRI (axial) — marked dilation of the lateral ventricles with mild sulcal enlargement, suggestive of NPH rather than neurodegenerative atrophy
CT head (axial) — dilation of the third and lateral ventricles with periventricular edema and disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid spaces (DESH)
Key Distinction: NPH vs. Hydrocephalus Ex Vacuo (HEV)

In NPH, a slow blockage of CSF drainage is the primary problem — ventricular enlargement subsequently causes brain resorption. In HEV, brain damage (stroke, trauma) causes primary brain shrinkage, and the ventricles enlarge secondarily to fill the space. This distinction matters: NPH may respond to shunting, HEV reflects irreversible volume loss that a shunt won't help.

4 · Treatment
Treatment

Mainstay is ventricular shunting — most commonly a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt, draining excess CSF from the lateral ventricle into the peritoneal cavity via a valve-regulated catheter tunneled under the skin.

Left: core NPH symptoms (dementia, urinary incontinence, magnetic gait) linked to ↓CSF absorption and ventriculomegaly. Right: VP shunt anatomy — ventricular catheter, shunt valve, catheter tunneled under the skin, terminating in the peritoneal cavity
5 · Monitoring & Complications
Monitoring & Complications

Shunt infections are the primary complication to monitor for following VP shunt placement.

Pearl

Gait is typically the first symptom to appear and the most responsive to shunting — which is exactly why gait improvement after the CSF tap test is the best available predictor of surgical benefit.

🦵 Restless Leg Syndrome

▶
▶ 2-Minute Neuroscience: Restless Legs Syndrome
Video — "2-Minute Neuroscience: Restless Legs Syndrome" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 34-year-old woman reports several months of an uncomfortable, crawling sensation deep in both legs that occurs almost every evening as she tries to fall asleep. The sensation is partially relieved by getting up and walking around, but returns as soon as she sits back down. Her husband has noticed her legs twitching throughout the night. She has no other neurologic symptoms, and her mother has similar complaints. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A common, chronic movement disorder causing a restless, non-painful urge to move the lower extremities, which also affects sleep. Synonyms: RLS, Willis-Ekbom disease, Ekbom syndrome, anxietas tibiarum.

  • Affects up to 10–15% of the general US population (>3 million cases); benign, idiopathic, can persist for years
  • Sex distribution reported inconsistently across sources — some cite female predominance, others near-equal prevalence
  • Peak incidence 30–40 years; can begin at any age (even infancy, often misdiagnosed as "growing pains" in children); most severely affected patients are middle-aged or older
  • Often not diagnosed until 10–20 years after symptom onset; progresses in ~2/3 of patients and can become disabling
Etiology & Pathophysiology

Primary RLS

  • Idiopathic; familial in up to 77% of cases
  • Onset typically <45y; progressive

Secondary RLS

  • Onset typically >45y; tied to an underlying condition or drug

Secondary causes: iron deficiency ± anemia, folate/magnesium/vitamin deficiency, uremia (end-stage renal disease), diabetic peripheral neuropathy, inflammatory conditions (celiac, RA, IBD), fibromyalgia, venous insufficiency, psychiatric conditions (depression, anxiety), neurological disease (Parkinson's, MS, polyneuropathies, spinal cord disease), pregnancy, emotional stress.

Pathophysiology remains unclear, but three interplaying factors are implicated: brain iron deficiency (impaired iron homeostasis, especially in the substantia nigra), dopamine dysfunction, and genetic predisposition. Peripheral contributions may include abnormal A fibers and altered peripheral nerve microvasculature.

Pathology, causes, primary vs. secondary types, and risk factors overview
2 · Clinical Presentation
Main Features — 4 Essential Criteria

A recurrent urge to move the legs that is:

  • Relieved by movement
  • Triggered and/or worsened by rest
  • Worse in the evening and at night (may occur exclusively at night)
  • Often accompanied by uncomfortable sensations — pain, pins and needles, itching, tickling, crawling, aching, or burning, typically in the calves/thighs, bilaterally (legs/feet more than arms)
Other Features
  • Periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS) or wakefulness (PLMW) are common — nighttime leg twitching
  • Other sleep disorders may coexist (e.g. insomnia → daytime drowsiness)
  • Secondary RLS patients may show signs of the underlying disease (e.g. Parkinson's or kidney failure findings)
  • Aggravating factors: H1 antihistamines (common in OTC sleep aids), dopamine antagonists (neuroleptics, metoclopramide), psychiatric medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs), lithium, beta blockers
Signs/symptoms and aggravating factors (diagnosis/treatment content on this slide is beyond this LO's core scope — see pearl below for a brief summary)
Diagnosis & Treatment Context

Beyond this LO's core scope: RLS is mainly a clinical diagnosis. Workup includes iron studies (ferritin) and CBC, with polysomnography if PLMS assessment is needed. Treatment starts with correcting reversible causes (e.g. oral iron if ferritin ≤75 ng/mL) and lifestyle changes; pharmacotherapy for chronic persistent RLS favors alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin) first-line, with low-dose dopamine agonists second-line; carbidopa/levodopa or benzodiazepines are options for intermittent symptoms, and low-dose opioids are reserved for refractory cases.

Pearl

All 4 essential features — urge to move (usually with uncomfortable sensations), worse with rest, relieved by movement, worse at night — should be present for a confident RLS diagnosis. Missing the circadian or rest-triggered pattern should make you reconsider.

😯 Tourette's Syndrome

▶
▶ Tourette's syndrome & tic disorders - definition, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment
Video — "Tourette's syndrome & tic disorders - definition, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 6-year-old boy is brought to his pediatrician because his mother has noticed him "acting strange" for over a year — rapid head jerking and frequent sniffing that occur many times a day, worsening during stressful periods. She notices him trying to suppress the movements beforehand and appearing relieved afterward. Neurologic exam is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A non-lethal neurodevelopmental disorder involving D2 receptors in the ventral corpus striatum of the basal ganglia, producing motor and phonic tic disorders of varying severity. Synonyms: Gilles de la Tourette Syndrome, TS.

  • The most common form of tic disorder
  • Annual incidence is low (~0.46/100,000), but because the disease is non-lethal, prevalence is high — 0.3–1% of the general population
  • Diagnosis is more common in boys (~4:1), but longer symptom persistence in females means overall prevalence ends up higher in girls
  • Mean age of tic onset ~5.6 years
Etiology & Pathogenesis
  • ~85–90% of patients have a comorbid neuropsychiatric condition: ADHD (~60%), OCD (~27%), and impulse control disorders
  • Mechanism unclear — likely a complex interaction of genetic, environmental, and social factors
  • Evidence supports a major-gene inheritance pattern with low penetrance and modifier genes, though no single specific gene has been confirmed; several candidate genes have been proposed
  • Abnormal reinforcement of a learned behavior via cortico-striatal pathways, with evidence pointing to dopaminergic overactivity, particularly in the ventral striatum (this mesolimbic circuit link is also why dopamine blockers work as treatment)
Pathology
  • Reduced frontal lobe size
  • Reduced global connections to the frontal lobes
Overview — pathology/causes, tic types, diagnosis, and treatment (diagnosis/treatment content previewed here is detailed further in sections 3–4 below)
2 · Clinical Presentation
Tics — The Hallmark of TS

Tics are brief, repetitive, purposeless, stereotyped actions with sudden onset and a waxing and waning course. A premonitory urge precedes the tic and is relieved once the tic is performed. Neurologic exam is otherwise normal.

Motor Tics

  • Eye blinking, body gyrations, head jerking
  • Echopraxia — repeating others' movements
  • Copropraxia — obscene gestures

Vocal Tics

  • Simple noises (e.g. sniffing, throat clearing)
  • Echolalia — repeating others' words/phrases; Palilalia — repeating one's own words
  • Coprolalia — blurting inappropriate/obscene language

Simple tics: short, involve one particular body part. Complex tics: multiple simultaneous tics.

Differential Diagnosis
  • Transient motor/phonic tic disorder: lasts <1 year (vs. ≥1 year required for TS)
  • Myoclonus, dystonia, chorea, stereotypies
  • Spasmus nutans — often confused with TS/a behavioral disorder, but distinguished by congenital nystagmus (horizontal, vertical, or rotary) with compensatory head bobbing and torticollis

Complications: reduced quality of life; often comorbid with anxiety and depression.

3 · Diagnostic Testing
Diagnostic Approach — DSM-5 Criteria

History and physical exam are key to diagnosis. DSM-5 requires all of the following:

  • ≥2 motor tics AND ≥1 vocal tic (need not occur concurrently)
  • Tics persist ≥1 year since the first tic (may wax and wane in frequency)
  • Onset <18 years of age
  • Not attributable to another cause (e.g. substance use, or a medical condition such as Huntington disease)
4 · Treatment
Treatment

Conservative

  • Behavioral therapy — habit reversal training, CBT
  • First-line for moderate, impairing tics or responsive comorbid psychiatric conditions

Medical

  • Antipsychotics (dopamine blockers) — risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone, aripiprazole, haloperidol, pimozide — reserved for severe cases
  • Tetrabenazine; α-2 adrenergic agonists (clonidine, guanfacine)
  • Botox injections may reduce facial tic appearance

Operative

  • Deep brain stimulation — early success, but reserved for refractory cases; larger trials still needed
Pearl — Prognosis Context

Tics typically decline during adolescence — around 50% of affected children see resolution by age 18; when tics persist into adulthood, severity often continues to decline over time.

🕳️ Syringomyelia

▶
▶ Syringomyelia (Year of the Zebra)
Video — "Syringomyelia (Year of the Zebra)" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 34-year-old man presents with a several-year history of gradually worsening weakness and clumsiness in both hands, along with odd numbness — he recently noticed a burn on his forearm that he hadn't felt happen. On exam he has bilateral hand and forearm muscle atrophy with reduced reflexes in the upper extremities, but preserved light touch and proprioception in the same distribution. Lower extremities show mild spasticity and hyperreflexia. MRI reveals a fluid-filled cavity within the cervical spinal cord. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A syrinx is a fluid-filled cavity (cyst) that develops within the spinal cord; as it expands, it produces a central cord syndrome. Results from disrupted CSF drainage from the central canal — commonly from a Chiari malformation or prior spinal trauma. If the syrinx extends into the brainstem, it's termed syringobulbia.

  • Global prevalence ~8.4–9.0 per 100,000
  • Sex: male > female, especially in trauma/SCI-related syringomyelia
  • Typical age range 30–40 years (SCI-related syringomyelia can occur at any age)
Etiology
  • Chiari malformation, especially type I — the most common cause
  • Posttraumatic (3–4% of spinal cord injury patients develop symptomatic syringomyelia); trauma, especially whiplash, is a recognized risk factor
  • Postinflammatory (transverse myelitis, arachnoiditis) or postinfectious (meningitis)
  • Intramedullary tumors (ependymoma, hemangioblastoma); scoliosis; other congenital malformations (e.g. tethered spinal cord syndrome)
  • Idiopathic in a significant proportion; may arise from an incompletely closed neural tube; single-gene mutations have been associated
Pathophysiology & Pathology
Obstructed central canal (usually cervical)
→
Impaired CSF drainage
→
Dilated fluid-filled syrinx forms
→
Compresses anterior white commissure
→
Damages crossing lateral spinothalamic fibers first

Further expansion may damage: anterior horn LMNs at segment level (→ bilateral flaccid paresis, atrophy) → lateral corticospinal tract UMNs (→ spastic paresis below the lesion) → descending hypothalamic fibers T1–T4 (→ Horner syndrome) → posterior columns in advanced disease (→ loss of position/vibration sense in the feet — this is typically the last structure affected) → medulla (→ syringobulbia).

Syringomyelia vs. hydromyelia: true syringomyelia is a cavity opening within the white matter, filled with extracellular fluid. Hydromyelia is a dilation of the central canal itself, filled with CSF, maintaining a connection to the 4th ventricle.

A syrinx (fluid-filled cyst) within the spinal cord — may be present at birth but remain clinically silent until early adulthood
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Most lesions occur between C2 and T9. Often asymptomatic and/or slowly progressing, with an insidious onset (similar to central cord syndrome).

  • Dissociated sensory loss in a cape-like distribution (neck, shoulders, arms) — loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch and proprioception; dysesthetic pain
  • Muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and areflexia at the lesion level (claw hand deformity possible)
  • Spastic paraparesis of the lower limbs may occur (below the lesion)
  • Autonomic disturbances: Horner syndrome, anhidrosis, bladder/bowel dysfunction, erectile dysfunction
  • Respiratory insufficiency; head/neck/back pain
  • Other: painless ulcers of the hands, Charcot joints, thoracic scoliosis
Syringobulbia (Brainstem Extension)

Tongue atrophy, loss of pain/temperature sensation in the trigeminal distribution, nystagmus, dysphagia, palatal and pharyngeal weakness.

3 · Diagnostic Testing
Diagnostic Approach
  • X-ray or CT: detects scoliosis and assesses the bony spine
  • MRI — confirmatory test: detects the syrinx (may be septated) and adjacent spinal cord lesions (e.g. tumors, arachnoiditis adhesions)
T2 MRI (sagittal) — a hyperintense syrinx spanning much of the cervical spinal column (T2-weighted cord normally appears hypointense)
Differential Diagnosis — Distinguishing Incomplete Cord Syndromes

Cervical disk prolapse, ALS, MS, and other incomplete spinal cord syndromes should all be considered. Two key ones to distinguish by pattern:

Brown-Séquard Syndrome

  • Asymmetric hemicord pattern — ipsilateral proprioception/motor loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss a few levels below the lesion
Brown-Séquard — asymmetric, single-limb-predominant pattern with dorsal column involvement

Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome

  • Bilateral, acute/subacute onset; dorsal columns (proprioception/vibration) spared entirely
ASA syndrome — bilateral pattern, dorsal columns spared, vascular (not central-cavity) mechanism

Syringomyelia differs from both: it's bilateral and symmetric like ASA syndrome, but unlike ASA syndrome, dorsal columns are not permanently spared — they can eventually become involved in advanced disease, since syringomyelia is a slowly expanding central cavity rather than a vascular event.

Pearl

Order of tract involvement as a syrinx expands: lateral spinothalamic tract first (crossing fibers at the anterior white commissure — pain/temperature) → anterior horn LMNs → lateral corticospinal tract → descending hypothalamic fibers (Horner) → dorsal columns last. Dorsal column signs = advanced disease.
